passages.text: In determining the energy savings from taxation-related policy measures introduced under Article 10, the following principles shall apply: (a) credit shall be given only for energy savings from taxation measures exceeding the minimum levels of taxation applicable to fuels as required in Council Directive 2003/96/EC (2) or 2006/112/EC (3); (b) short-run price elasticities for the calculation of the impact of the energy taxation measures shall represent the responsiveness of energy demand to price changes, and shall be estimated on the basis of recent and representative official data sources, which are applicable for the Member State, and, where applicable, on the basis of accompanying studies from an independent institute.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: If a different price elasticity than short-run elasticities is used, Member States shall explain how energy efficiency improvements due to the implementation of other Union legislation have been included in the baseline used to estimate the energy savings, or how a double-counting of energy savings from other Union legislation has been avoided; (c) the energy savings from accompanying taxation policy instruments, including fiscal incentives or payment to a fund, shall be accounted separately; (d) short-run elasticity estimates should be used to assess the energy savings from taxation measures to avoid overlap with Union law and other policy measures; (e) Member States shall determine distributional effects of taxation and equivalent measures on people affected by energy poverty, vulnerable customers and, where applicable, people living in social housing, and show the effects of the mitigation measures implemented in accordance with Article 24(1), (2) and (3); (f) Member States shall provide evidence, including calculation methodologies, that where there is an overlap in the impact of energy or carbon taxation measures or emissions trading in accordance with Directive 2003/87/EC, there is no double counting of energy savings.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: (f) policy measures or programmes or measures financed under a national energy efficiency fund implemented as a priority among people affected by energy poverty, vulnerable customers and, where applicable, people living in social housing; (g) the share and the amount of energy savings to be achieved among people affected by energy poverty, vulnerable customers and, where applicable, people living in social housing; (h) where applicable, the indicators applied, the arithmetic average share and the outcome of policy measures established pursuant to Article 8(3); (i) where applicable, impacts and adverse effects of policy measures implemented pursuant to Article 8(3) on people affected by energy poverty, vulnerable customers and, where applicable, people living in social housing; (j) the duration of the obligation period for the energy efficiency obligation scheme; (k) where applicable, the amount of energy savings or cost reduction targets to be achieved by obligated parties among people affected by energy poverty, vulnerable customers and, where applicable, people living in social housing; (l) the actions provided for by the policy measure; (m) the calculation methodology, including how additionality and materiality have been determined and which methodologies and benchmarks are used for deemed and scaled savings, and, where applicable, the net calorific values and conversion factors used; (n) the lifetimes of measures, and how they are calculated or what they are based upon; (o) the approach taken to address climatic variations within the Member State; (p) the monitoring and verification systems for measures under Articles 9 and 10 and how their independence from the obligated, participating or entrusted parties is ensured; (q) in the case of taxation: (i) the target sectors and segment of taxpayers; (ii) the implementing public authority; (iii) the savings expected to be achieved; (iv) the duration of the taxation measure; (v) the calculation methodology, including the price elasticities used and how they have been established and (vi) how overlaps with EU ETS in accordance with Directive 2003/87/EC have been avoided and the risk of double counting has been abolished.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: ANNEX VI MINIMUM CRITERIA FOR ENERGY AUDITS INCLUDING THOSE CARRIED OUT AS PART OF ENERGY MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS The energy audits referred to in Article 11 shall: (a) be based on up-to-date, measured, traceable operational data on energy consumption and (for electricity) load profiles; (b) comprise a detailed review of the energy consumption profile of buildings or groups of buildings, industrial operations or installations, including transportation; (c) identify energy efficiency measures to decrease energy consumption; (d) identify the potential for cost-effective use or production of renewable energy; (e) build, whenever possible, on life-cycle cost analysis instead of simple payback periods in order to take account of longterm savings, residual values of long-term investments and discount rates; (f) be proportionate, and sufficiently representative to permit the drawing of a reliable picture of overall energy performance and the reliable identification of the most significant opportunities for improvement.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: Energy audits shall allow detailed and validated calculations for the proposed measures so as to provide clear information on potential savings. The data used in energy audits shall be storable for historical analysis and tracking performance. 2023 L 231/89

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: ANNEX VII MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS FOR MONITORING AND PUBLISHING THE ENERGY PERFORMANCE OF DATA CENTRES The following minimum information shall be monitored and published with regard to the energy performance of data centres referred to in Article 12: (a) the name of the data centre, the name of the owner and operators of the data centre, the date on which the data centre started its operations and the municipality where the data centre is based; (b) the floor area of the data centre, the installed power, the annual incoming and outgoing data traffic, and the amount of data stored and processed within the data centre; (c) the performance, during the last full calendar year, of the data centre in accordance with key performance indicators about, inter alia, energy consumption, power utilisation, temperature set points, waste heat utilisation, water usage and use of renewable energy, using as a basis, where applicable, the CEN/CENELEC EN 50600-4 ‘Information technology – Data centre facilities and infrastructures’, until the entry into force of the delegated act adopted pursuant to Article 33(3).

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: ANNEX VIII MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS FOR BILLING AND BILLING INFORMATION BASED ON ACTUAL CONSUMPTION OF NATURAL GAS 1. 1. Billing based on actual consumption In order to enable final customers to regulate their own energy consumption, billing should take place on the basis of actual consumption at least once a year, and billing information should be made available at least on a quarterly basis, on request or where the consumers have opted to receive electronic billing or else twice a year. Gas used only for cooking purposes may be exempt from this requirement. 2.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: Minimum information contained in the bill Member States shall ensure that, where appropriate, the following information is made available to final customers in clear and understandable terms in or with their bills, contracts, transactions, and receipts at distribution stations: (a) current actual prices and actual consumption of energy; (b) comparisons of the final customer’s current energy consumption with consumption for the same period in the previous year, preferably in graphic form; (c) contact information for final customers’ organisations, energy agencies or similar bodies, including website addresses from which information may be obtained on available energy efficiency improvement measures, comparative end-user profiles and objective technical specifications for energy-using equipment.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: In addition, wherever possible and useful, Member States shall ensure that comparisons with an average normalised or benchmarked final customer in the same user category are made available to final customers in clear and understandable terms, in, with or signposted to within, their bills, contracts, transactions, and receipts at distribution stations. 3.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: Advice on energy efficiency accompanying bills and other feedback to final customers When sending contracts and contract changes, and in the bills customers receive or through websites addressing individual customers, energy distributors, distribution system operators and retail energy sales companies shall inform their customers in a clear and understandable manner of contact information for independent consumer advice centres, energy agencies or similar institutions, including their internet addresses, where they can obtain advice on available energy efficiency measures, benchmark profiles for their energy consumption and technical specifications of energy using appliances that can serve to reduce the consumption of those appliances.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: Minimum frequency of billing or consumption information Until 31 December 2021, where remotely readable meters or heat cost allocators have been installed, billing or consumption information based on actual consumption or heat cost allocator readings shall be provided to final users at least on a quarterly basis upon request or where final customers have opted to receive electronic billing, or else twice a year. From 1 January 2022, where remotely readable meters or heat cost allocators have been installed, billing or consumption information based on actual consumption or heat cost allocator readings shall be provided to final users at least on a monthly basis.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: It may also be made available via the internet and be updated as frequently as allowed by the measurement devices and systems used. Heating and cooling may be exempted from that requirement outside the heating or cooling seasons. 3.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: Minimum information contained in the bill Member States shall ensure that the following information is made available to final users in clear and comprehensible terms in or with their bills where those are based on actual consumption or heat cost allocator readings: (a) current actual prices and actual consumption of energy or total heat cost and heat cost allocator readings; (b) the fuel mix used and the related annual GHG emissions, including for final users supplied by district heating or district cooling, and a description of the different taxes, levies and tariffs applied; (c) comparisons of the final users’ current energy consumption with consumption for the same period in the previous year, in graphic form and climate corrected for heating and cooling; (d) contact information for final customers’ organisations, energy agencies or similar bodies, including website addresses, from which information on available energy efficiency improvement measures, comparative end-user profiles and objective technical specifications for energy-using equipment may be obtained; (e) information about related complaints procedures, ombudsman services or alternative dispute resolution mechanisms, as applicable in the Member States; (f) comparisons with an average normalised or benchmarked final user in the same user category.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: In the case of electronic bills, such comparisons may instead be made available online and signposted to within the bills. Member States may limit the scope of the requirement to provide information about GHG emissions pursuant to point (b) of the first subparagraph to include only supplies from district heating systems with a total rated thermal input exceeding 20 MW. Bills that are not based on actual consumption or heat cost allocator readings shall contain a clear and comprehensible explanation of how the amount set out in the bill was calculated, and at least the information referred to in points (d) and (e). 2023

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: ANNEX X POTENTIAL FOR EFFICIENCY IN HEATING AND COOLING The comprehensive assessment of national heating and cooling potentials referred to in Article 25(1) shall include and shall be based on the following: Part I OVERVIEW OF HEATING AND COOLING 1. heating and cooling demand in terms of assessed useful energy (1) and quantified final energy consumption in GWh per year (2) by sector: (a) residential; (b) services; (c) industry; (d) any other sector that individually consumes more than 5 % of total national useful heating and cooling demand; 2.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: the identification, or, in the case of point (a)(i), the identification or estimation, of current heating and cooling supply: (a) by technology, in GWh per year (3), within the sectors referred to in point 1 where possible, distinguishing between energy derived from fossil and renewable sources: (i) provided on-site in residential and service sites by: — heat only boilers; — high-efficiency heat and power cogeneration; — heat pumps; — other on-site technologies and sources; (ii) provided on-site in non-service and non-residential sites by: — heat only boilers; — high-efficiency heat and power cogeneration; — heat pumps; — other on-site technologies and sources; (iii) provided off-site by: — high-efficiency heat and power cogeneration; — waste heat; — other off-site technologies and sources; (b) the identification of installations that generate waste heat or cold and their potential heating or cooling supply, in GWh per year: (i) thermal power generation installations that can supply or can be retrofitted to supply waste heat with a total thermal input exceeding 50 MW; (ii) heat and power cogeneration installations using technologies referred to in Part II of Annex II with a total thermal input exceeding 20 MW; (iii) waste incineration plants; (1) The amount of thermal energy needed to satisfy the heating and cooling demand of end-users.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: (2) The most recent data available should be used. (3) The most recent data available should be used. 2023 L 231/93

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: (iv) renewable energy installations with a total thermal input exceeding 20 MW other than the installations specified under points (i) and (ii) generating heating or cooling using the energy from renewable sources; (v) industrial installations with a total thermal input exceeding 20 MW which can provide waste heat; (c) reported share of energy from renewable sources and from waste heat or cold in the final energy consumption of the district heating and cooling (4) sector over the past 5 years, in accordance with Directive (EU) 2018/2001; 3.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: aggregated data on cogeneration units in existing district heating and cooling networks in five capacity ranges covering: (a) primary energy consumption; (b) overall efficiency; (c) primary energy savings; (d) CO2 emission factors; 4. aggregated data on existing district heating and cooling networks supplied from cogeneration in five capacity ranges covering: (a) overall primary energy consumption; (b) primary energy consumption of cogeneration units; (c) share of cogeneration in district heating or cooling supply; (d) district heating system losses; (e) district cooling system losses; (f) connection density; (g) shares of systems per different operating temperature groups; 5.

passages.text: a map covering the entire national territory, which, while preserving commercially sensitive information, identifies: (a) heating and cooling demand areas following from the analysis of point 1, while using consistent criteria for focusing on energy dense areas in municipalities and conurbations; (b) existing heating and cooling supply points identified under point 2(b) and district heating transmission installations; (c) planned heating and cooling supply points of the type described under point 2(b) and identified new areas for the district heating and cooling; 6.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: a forecast of trends in the demand for heating and cooling to maintain a perspective of the next 30 years in GWh and taking into account, in particular, projections for the next 10 years, the change in demand in buildings and different sectors of the industry, and the impact of policies and strategies related to the demand management, such as longterm building renovation strategies under Directive (EU) 2018/844 of the European Parliament and of the Council (5); (4) The identification of ‘renewable cooling’ shall, after the methodology for calculating the quantity of renewable energy used for cooling and district cooling is established in accordance with Article 35 of Directive (EU) 2018/2001, be carried out in accordance with that Directive.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: a general overview of the existing policies and measures as described in the most recent report submitted in accordance with Articles 3, 20 and 21 and Article 27(a) of Regulation (EU) 2018/1999; Part III ANALYSIS OF THE ECONOMIC POTENTIAL FOR EFFICIENCY IN HEATING AND COOLING 9. an analysis of the economic potential (6) of different technologies for heating and cooling shall be carried out for the entire national territory by using the cost-benefit analysis referred to in Article 25(3) and shall identify alternative scenarios for more efficient and renewable heating and cooling technologies, distinguishing between energy derived from fossil and renewable sources where applicable.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: The following technologies should be considered: (a) industrial waste heat and cold; (b) waste incineration; (c) high efficiency cogeneration; (d) renewable energy sources, such as geothermal, solar thermal and biomass, other than those used for high efficiency cogeneration; (e) heat pumps; (f) reducing heat and cold losses from existing district networks; (g) district heating and cooling; 10.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: the analysis of economic potential shall include the following steps and considerations: (a) Considerations: (i) the cost-benefit analysis for the purposes of Article 25(3) shall include an economic analysis that takes into consideration socioeconomic and environmental factors (7), and a financial analysis performed to assess projects from the investors’ point of view, both economic and financial analyses using the net present value as a criterion for the assessment; (ii) the baseline scenario should serve as a reference point and take into account existing policies at the time of compiling this comprehensive assessment (8), and be linked to data collected under Part I and Part II, point 6 of this Annex; (6) The analysis of the economic potential should present the volume of energy (in GWh) that can be generated per year by each technology analysed.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: The limitations and interrelations within the energy system should also be taken into account. The analysis may make use of models based on assumptions representing the operation of common types of technologies or systems. (7) Including the assessment referred to in Article 15 (7) of Directive (EU) 2018/2001. (8) The cut-off date for taking into account policies for the baseline scenario is the end of the year preceding to the year by the end of which the comprehensive assessment is due. That is to say, policies enacted within a year prior to the deadline for submission of the comprehensive assessment do not need to be taken into account. 2023 L 231/95

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: (iii) alternative scenarios to the baseline shall take into account energy efficiency and the renewable energy objectives of Regulation (EU) 2018/1999, each scenario presenting the following elements compared to the baseline scenario: — economic potential of technologies examined using the net present value as criterion; — GHG emission reductions; — primary energy savings in GWh per year; — impact on the share of renewables in the national energy mix. Scenarios that are not feasible due to technical reasons, financial reasons or national regulation may be excluded at an early stage of the cost-benefit analysis, if justified on the basis of careful, explicit and welldocumented considerations.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: The assessment and decision-making should take into account costs and energy savings from the increased flexibility in energy supply and from a more optimal operation of the electricity networks, including avoided costs and savings from reduced infrastructure investment, in the analysed scenarios.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: (b) Costs and benefits The costs and benefits referred to in point (a) shall include at least the following costs and benefits: (i) costs: — capital costs of plants and equipment; — capital costs of the associated energy networks; — variable and fixed operating costs; — energy costs; — environmental, health and safety costs, to the extent possible; — labour market costs, energy security and competitiveness, to the extent possible.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: (ii) benefits: — value of output to the consumer (heating, cooling and electricity); — external benefits such as environmental, greenhouse gas emissions and health and safety benefits, to the extent possible; — labour market effects, energy security and competitiveness, to the extent possible. (c) Relevant scenarios to the baseline: All relevant scenarios to the baseline shall be considered, including the role of efficient individual heating and cooling.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: The cost-benefit analysis may cover either a project assessment or a group of projects for a broader local, regional or national assessment in order to establish the most cost-effective and beneficial heating or cooling solution against a baseline for a given geographical area for the purpose of planning.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: (d) Boundaries and integrated approach: (i) the geographical boundary shall cover a suitable, well-defined geographical area; (ii) the cost-benefit analyses shall take into account all relevant centralised or decentralised supply resources available within the system and geographical boundary, including technologies considered under Part III, point 9, of this Annex, and heating and cooling demand trends and characteristics. 2023

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: (ii) the discount rate used in the economic analysis to calculate net present value shall be chosen according to European or national guidelines; (iii) Member States shall use national, European or international energy price development forecasts, if appropriate, in their national, regional or local context; (iv) the prices used in the economic analysis shall reflect socio-economic costs and benefits. External costs, such as environmental and health effects, should be included to the extent possible, namely when a market price exists or when it is already included in European or national regulation.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: (f) Sensitivity analysis: a sensitivity analysis shall be included to assess the costs and benefits of a project or group of projects and be based on variable factors having a significant impact on the outcome of the calculations, such as different energy prices, levels of demand, discount rates and other. Part IV POTENTIAL NEW STRATEGIES AND POLICY MEASURES 11.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: an overview of new legislative and non-legislative policy measures (9) to realise the economic potential identified in accordance with points 9 and 10, together with a forecast of: (a) greenhouse gas emission reductions; (b) primary energy savings in GWh per year; (c) impact on the share of high-efficiency cogeneration; (d) impact on the share of renewables in the national energy mix and in the heating and cooling sector; (e) links to national financial programming and cost savings for the public budget and market participants; (f) estimated public support measures, if any, with their annual budget and identification of the potential aid element.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: (9) This overview shall include financing measures and programmes that may be adopted over the period of the comprehensive assessment, not prejudging a separate notification of the public support schemes for a State aid assessment. 2023 L 231/97

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: ANNEX XI COST-BENEFIT ANALYSES Cost-benefit analyses shall provide information for the purpose of the measures referred to in Article 25(3) and Article 26(7): If an electricity-only installation or an installation without heat recovery is planned, a comparison shall be made between the planned installations or the planned refurbishment and an equivalent installation producing the same amount of electricity or process heat, but recovering the waste heat and supplying heat through high-efficiency cogeneration or district heating and cooling networks, or both.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: Within a given geographical boundary the assessment shall take into account the planned installation and any appropriate existing or potential heat or cooling demand points that could be supplied from it, taking into account rational possibilities, for example, technical feasibility and distance. The system boundary shall be set to include the planned installation and the heat and cooling loads, such as building(s) and industrial process. Within this system boundary the total cost of providing heat and power shall be determined for both cases and compared.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: Heat or cooling loads shall include existing heat or cooling loads, such as an industrial installation or an existing district heating or cooling system, and also, in urban areas, the heat or cooling load and costs that would exist if a group of buildings or part of a city were provided with or connected into a new district heating or cooling network, or both. Cost-benefit analyses shall be based on a description of the planned installation and the comparison installation(s), covering electrical and thermal capacity, as applicable, fuel type, planned usage and the number of planned operating hours every year, location and electricity and thermal demand.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: An assessment of waste heat utilisation shall take into consideration current technologies. The assessment shall take into consideration the direct use of waste heat or its upgrading to higher temperature levels, or both. In the case of waste heat recovery on-site, at least the use of heat exchangers, heat pumps, and heat to power technologies shall be assessed. In the case of waste heat recovery off-site, at least industrial installations, agriculture sites and district heating networks shall be assessed as potential demand points.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: For the purpose of the comparison, the thermal energy demand and the types of heating and cooling used by the nearby heat or cooling demand points shall be taken into account. The comparison shall cover infrastructure related costs for the planned and comparison installation. Cost-benefit analyses for the purposes of Article 26(7) shall include an economic analysis covering a financial analysis reflecting actual cash flow transactions from investing in and operating individual installations. Projects with positive cost-benefit outcome are those where the sum of discounted benefits in the economic and financial analysis exceeds the sum of discounted costs (cost-benefit surplus).

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: Member States shall set guiding principles for the methodology, assumptions and time horizon for the economic analysis. Member States may require that the companies responsible for the operation of thermal electric generation installations, industrial companies, district heating and cooling networks, or other parties influenced by the defined system boundary and geographical boundary, contribute data for use in assessing the costs and benefits of an individual installation. 2023

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: ANNEX XII GUARANTEE OF ORIGIN FOR ELECTRICITY PRODUCED FROM HIGH-EFFICIENCY COGENERATION (1) Member States shall take measures to ensure that: (a) the guarantee of origin of the electricity produced from high-efficiency cogeneration: — enables producers to demonstrate that the electricity they sell is produced from high-efficiency cogeneration and is issued to that effect in response to a request from the producer; — is accurate, reliable and fraud-resistant; — is issued, transferred and cancelled electronically; (b) the same unit of energy from high-efficiency cogeneration is taken into account only once.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: (2) The guarantee of origin referred to in Article 26(13) shall contain at least the following information: (a) the identity, location, type and capacity (thermal and electrical) of the installation where the energy was produced; (b) the dates and places of production; (c) the lower calorific value of the fuel source from which the electricity was produced; (d) the quantity and the use of the heat generated together with the electricity; (e) the quantity of electricity from high-efficiency cogeneration in accordance with Annex III that the guarantee of origin represents; (f) the primary energy savings calculated in accordance with Annex III on the basis of the harmonised efficiency reference values indicated in Annex III, point (d); (g) the nominal electric and thermal efficiency of the plant; (h) whether and to what extent the installation has benefited from investment support; (i) whether and to what extent the unit of energy has benefited in any other way from a national support scheme, and the type of support scheme; (j) the date on which the installation became operational; and (k) the date and country of issue and a unique identification number.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: The guarantee of origin shall be of the standard size of 1 MWh. It shall relate to the net electricity output measured at the station boundary and exported to the grid. 2023 L 231/99

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: Network regulation and tariffs shall not prevent network operators or energy retailers making available system services for demand response measures, demand management and distributed generation on organised electricity markets, including over-the-counter markets and electricity exchanges for trading energy, capacity, balancing and ancillary services in all timeframes, including forward, day-ahead and intra-day markets, in particular: (a) the shifting of the load from peak to off-peak times by final customers taking into account the availability of renewable energy, energy from cogeneration and distributed generation; (b) energy savings from demand response of distributed consumers by independent aggregators; (c) demand reduction from energy efficiency measures undertaken by energy service providers, including ESCOs; (d) the connection and dispatch of generation sources at lower voltage levels; (e) the connection of generation sources from closer location to the consumption; and (f) the storage of energy.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: 3. Network or retail tariffs may support dynamic pricing for demand response measures by final customers, such as: (a) time-of-use tariffs; (b) critical peak pricing; (c) real time pricing; and (d) peak time rebates. 2023

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: ANNEX XIV ENERGY EFFICIENCY REQUIREMENTS FOR TRANSMISSION SYSTEM OPERATORS AND DISTRIBUTION SYSTEM OPERATORS Transmission system operators and distribution system operators shall: (a) set up and make public their standard rules relating to the bearing and sharing of costs of technical adaptations, such as grid connections, grid reinforcements and the introduction of new grids, improved operation of the grid and rules on the non-discriminatory implementation of the grid codes, which are necessary in order to integrate new producers feeding electricity produced from high-efficiency cogeneration into the interconnected grid; (b) provide any new producer of electricity produced from high-efficiency cogeneration wishing to be connected to the system with the comprehensive and necessary information required, including: (i) a comprehensive and detailed estimate of the costs associated with the connection; (ii) a reasonable and precise timetable for receiving and processing the request for grid connection; (iii) a reasonable indicative timetable for any proposed grid connection.

passages.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast, 13 September 2023)
passages.text: The overall process to become connected to the grid should be no longer than 24 months, bearing in mind what is reasonably practicable and nondiscriminatory; (c) provide standardised and simplified procedures for the connection of distributed high-efficiency cogeneration producers to facilitate their connection to the grid. The standard rules referred to in point (a) of the first paragraph shall be based on objective, transparent and nondiscriminatory criteria taking particular account of all the costs and benefits associated with the connection of those producers to the grid. passages.text: Fraunhofer ISI | 9 1 Introduction The successful implementation of the recast Energy Efficiency Directive (EED) is crucial for achieving the European Union's energy efficiency, clean energy transition and sustainability goals. However, translating policy objectives into concrete measures can be complex and challenging for Member States. The legislative text of the EED serves as the primary legal framework, setting out the necessary obligations, targets and timetables for Member States to follow when implementing energy efficiency measures. The guidance notes adopted by the European Commission aim to support Member States in the transposition and implementation of the EED.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: Good practices serve as valuable references and sources of inspiration for Member States in their efforts to design and implement effective energy efficiency measures. T his practical report thus presents exemplary initiatives in various Member States, highlighting innovative approaches, best practices, and lessons learned. By providing examples, this report helps Member States understand how concrete solutions have been used to translate legal requirements into effective and impactful energy efficiency policies. In this report, we will explore and analyse a wide range of good practices related to the different articles of the recast EED.

passages.text: Good practice example of EE1st application in planning decisions: Integrated heating and cooling planning in Munich, Germany18,19 There are several recent and notable examples of integrated heating and cooling planning in European municipalities that demonstrate good practice in applying the EE1st principle by focusing on enduse energy efficiency in buildings, the use of renewable e nergy sources and the optimisation of existing infrastructure. Among these, Munich's Integrated Heating and Cooling Plan20 stands out as a strategic initiative in line with the city's broader ambition to reduce CO2 emissions and transition to sustainable energy.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: Central to Munich's strategy is the expansion of its district heating network. The plan focuses on replacing coal-fired heating plants with more sustainable options, such as large-scale heat pumps and thermal storage. Improving the energy efficiency of exi sting buildings is another key aspect. Retrofitting buildings to reduce energy demand demonstrates Munich's commitment to the EE1st principle, prioritising the reduction of energy consumption as a primary objective. Implementing Munich's plan involves overcoming challenges, in particular balancing the expansion of the heating network with environmental and urban considerations.

passages.text: Fraunhofer ISI | 17 schemes can incorporate and support the monitoring of achievements against national energy efficiency regulations/goals. Croatia has established an M&V scheme in the form of an IT -tool called System for Monitoring, Measurement and Verification of Energy Savings (SMIV) in line with the Croatian National Energy Efficiency Action. The SMIV involves the participation of parties at all levels (local, regional, national) across the public sector, the household sector, the industry sector and the transport sector, and is used to calculate energy savings in three main sectors: building, industry, and transport.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: The SMIV specifically reports on the energy and cost savings from energy renovation programmes for public buildings. The SMIV began as a project developed in cooperation with GIZ and subsequently became the official national M&V tool through the Croatian Energy Efficiency Act of 2014. With this tool, Croatia is reporting energy savings as required in the EED.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: The SMIV calculates energy savings using dominantly deemed savings or engineering estimates. This allows all users to generate reports, plans and calculations of their energy savings under a unified methodology. The measured energy savings are verified through algorithms in SMIV. Targets for each measure in SMIV are related to those same measures planned through the NEEAP. Documentation proving the energy savings must be uploaded in SMIV for verification by the National Energy Efficiency Authority. Data con tained in SMIV is used for many energy savings calculations, analysis and the continuous overview of achieved national energy efficiency targets.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)

They were officially proposed and then adopted by the Minister of Economy.

passages.text: The example of Denmark's EEOS shows the difficulty to balance monitoring and verification on the one hand and the associated cost and administrative burden on the other hand. In Denmark, the target was raised several times, and the obligated parties were overachieving. These centralised M&V systems allow to directly track and correct for double counting. It also ensures that harmonised calculation methods are used across all policy measures, creating consistency in the energy savings data. In both countries, the M&V system is operated by a dedicated body (monitoring body in Austria; national coordination body for energy efficiency in Croatia).

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: Such centralised M&V systems require an investment cost, constant management, and regular updates. It has proven to be effective to get regular updates about policy measures’ achievements and progress towards targets. They provide useful information for steering the policy measures and a rapid feedback loop to detect needs for adjustments in M&V rules and other design features of the policy measures. Centralised systems also help optimizing controls when needed. Therefore, these centralised M&V systems come at a significant cost, but also deliver high benefits for policy making and effectiveness .

passages.text: 1 Introduction Article 21 of the EED Recast aims at strengthening the position of consumers by introducing basic contractual rights for the supply of heating, cooling and domestic hot water, in line with the rights set out in Directive 2009/73/EG regarding the provision of gas services and Directive 2019/944 regarding the provision of electricity. Stakeholder involvement, including energy suppliers, consumer groups, and regulators, is crucial in the early stages of this transposition process to address specific challenges and national differences.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: In this report, we present the findings of an exhaustive analysis aimed at identifying good practice examples in accordance with the requirements of Article 21. Our research delved into the current practices across various countries, with a particular emphasis on supply of other forms of energy and industries closely related to the energy sector, such as the telecommunications sector. This choice of industries provided comparative data, allowing us to draw meaningful parallels and insights. Central to our investigation was an indepth examination of contract design.

Furthermore, our study paid special attention to the mechanisms in place for handling complaints and resolving disputes. By analysing how these industries manage customer grievances and disputes, we gained valuable perspectives on effective resolution strategies that prioritise fairness and customer satisfaction.

Good practices presented in this chapter concern two specific obligations: (1) the creation of One -Stop-Shops (OSS) or similar mechanisms and (2) addressing the issue of split incentives between owners and tenants. Below we group good practices for each of the four business models identified for OSS for integrated home energy renovations.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: 1 Introduction Article 24 of the EED Recast creates a new obligation for Member States to take appropriate measures to empower and protect people affected by energy poverty, vulnerable customers, lowincome households and, where applicable, people living in social housing. This chapter presents good practices related to ringfencing budgets and offering higher subsidy levels to low-income or vulnerable households. It brings examples on supporting landlords of rented buildings and capacity buildings for the intervening specialists. 1 What are distributional effects?

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: The distributional effects of policies and measures are crucial to take into consideration when designing them, as this will determine how different segments of the population, in particular households or individuals of different income levels, are impacted. Anticipating these impacts is crucial for proactively addressing potential disparities and inequities resulting from the implementation of policies. This is important to enable policymakers to design and implement policies and measures that promote a more just and inclusive society.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: Negative distributional impacts: Negative distributional impacts occur when policies and measures disproportionately affect people in energy poverty, vulnerable customers, low -income households and, where applicable, people living in social housing215. For example, policies that lead to price increases in essential goods and services, such as energy, can have regressive effects. Low-income households, which spend a larger proportion of their income on these necessities, bear a heavier burden compared to higher-income households216. This can deepen poverty and perpetuate income di sparities, widening the gap between the rich and the poor.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: Positive distributional Impacts: On the contrary, policies and measures that benefit the listed vulnerable groups can be considered as positive or progressive 217. Such policies and measures frequently encompass targeted social programmes, income transfers, or measures aimed to enhance access to essential services for this target group. A range of policies and measures are used by Member States to mitigate distributional effects, including structural tax ref orms, financial payments or cashback, investments in technology or equipment at the individual/household level, or investments in public service/infrastructure to 215 Pizer, W. , & Sexton, S. (2019).

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: Fraunhofer ISI | 98 benefit the most burdened groups or communities. Investments in energy efficiency measures at the household level, as targeted by Article 24 of the recast EED, and in some cases in public services and infrastructure, are particularly relevant to help mitigate negative distributional impacts of policies and measures that increase energy bills or other energy -related burdens.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: Whereas measures to increase income or help to pay energy bills provide support only in the year they are offered, energy efficiency investments provide more sustainable solutions and help to address the structural inequalities that lead to the negative distributional impacts, like inefficient homes and access to only expensive, inefficient, or polluting energy sources218 . To support the assessment of distributional impacts , the Commission provided Guidance in 2022 (COM/2022/494) on better assessing the distributional impact of Member States policies219 .

passages.text: 2 Energy Efficiency Obligation Scheme The Energy Efficiency Obligation Scheme (EEOS) in Ireland 220 is an ongoing programme administered by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) that obligates energy suppliers and distributors to deliver energy savings. Under the EEOS, the obligated parties have specific targets that can be reached by offering support and incentives to improve the energy efficiency of homes and businesses. F or each unit of energy saved, obligated parties earn energy credits that count towards their targets. All energy types, including electricity, gas, and solid fuel, are included in the scheme.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: Launched in 2014, the scheme has undergone revisions and upd ates, including an increase in residential deemed credits. What makes the energy efficiency obligation scheme a good practice? The Energy Efficiency Obligation Scheme (EEOS) acknowledges that energy costs can place a disproportionate burden on low -income households. By means of ‘ringfencing’ the scheme allocates a minimum percentage of 5% of the total energy savings to the benefit of low-income or vulnerable households. This mechanism addresses the impact of the costs being passed on to customer bills and promotes energy saving measures being implemented as a priority for low - income or vuln erable households.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: The prioritisation of e nergy savings measures allows these households to reduce energy bills, increase indoor comfort, and improve energy affordability. So, the EEOS effectively reduces the energy burden and promotes equitable access to efficient energy resources for all citizens. The implementation of Energy Efficiency Obligation Schemes (EEOS) in various Member States has demonstrated a pattern of gradual introduction, learning, and redesign. In countries like Italy and Denmark, the schemes underwent a learning process before significant savings targets were established. However, new EEOS schemes offer opportunities to expedite the delivery of significant energy savings.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: 3 Financial assistance programme for homeowners "MaPrimeRénov Sérénité" in France 222 is a government programme aimed at promoting energy renovation and improving the energy efficiency of homes. Launched in 2020, the programme provides financial assistance to homeowners to undertake energy-saving renovations and upgrades in their properties. The programme offers a comprehensive support package, including financial aid, technical guidance, and assistance throughout the renovation process. The programme targets both in dividual homeowners and condominiums, with different funding options available depending on income level and the type of renovation.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: The financial aid provided through the programme is financed by energy suppliers as a way to fulfil their obligations under the Natio nal White Certificate or “Certificat d’Économie d’Énergie (CEE)”223 programme. What makes the financial assistance programme for homeowners a good practice? In response to the challenges faced by low-income households in accessing and affording energy savings upgrades, the "MaPrimeRénov Sérénité" programme incorporates various measures to address these challenges. One important aspect is the allocation of higher subsidy levels, in particular for low-income households, ensuring that they receive increased financial support.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: In addition, the National White Certificates Scheme aims to ensure that 25% of the White Certificates are generated to benefit low-income households. The programme also offers technical assistance throughout the renovation process and simplifies the application process, making it easier for vulnerable households to participate. These households are given priority access, ensuring they can benefit from the programme's resources. Additionally, "MaPrimeRénov Sérénité" provides information about other eligible funding schemes and collaborates with local authorities and community organi sations to establish a comprehensive support network.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: By combining ringfencing, higher subsidy levels for low -income households, and information measures, "MaPrimeRénov Sérénité" effectively supports and protects vulnerable groups. It strives to remove barriers, provide financial assistance, and ensure equita ble access to energy -saving measures for those who need it the most. As part of the broader strategy to optimi se energy consumption of energy poor households, MaPrimeRénov Sérénité is complemented by additional longterm initiatives that include educational programmes aimed to better promote energy usage practices within households. Additionally, direct income support measures are implemented to alleviate the burden of energy bills.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: 3 Good practice on public funding - Home energy efficiency programme The Home Energy Efficiency Programmes for Scotland (HEEPS) 225 offer financial assistance and incentives to homeowners and tenants to make their properties more energy -efficient, reduce carbon emissions, and lower energy bills. HEEPS is primarily funded by the Scottish Gov ernment and implemented through various agencies and market actors such as local authorities and energy efficiency organisations. These entities collaborate closely with homeowners, providing guidance, evaluating eligibility, and administering funding and incentives to facilitate energy efficiency measures.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: The programme focuses on concrete measures to enhance energy efficiency, including insulation upgrades such as loft or cavity wall insulation, the installation of efficient heating systems like boilers or heat pumps, and the adoption of renewable energy technologies like solar panels. In addition to financial assistance, HEEPS provides energy advice and raises awareness on energy efficiency measures. It offers resources and information to homeowners, enabli ng them to understand energy efficiency options, reduce energy consumption, and make informed decisions about their homes. What makes the home energy efficiency programme a good practice?

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: The Scottish HEEPS combine national funds for energy efficiency and heat with top-up funding for costly measures based on the local area, along with a zero-interest loan. The programmes include targeted schemes and initiatives for low -income and vulnerable households to tackle energy poverty and improve the energy efficiency of their homes. One of these schemes is the Warmer Homes Scotland programme226, which provides tailored support to eligible households. Warmer Homes Scotland offers free energy efficiency measures and improvements to eligible households, including insulation, heating system upgrades, and renewable energy installations.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: It is designed to make homes warmer, more comfortable, and more affordable to heat, particularly for those facing energy poverty. The HEEPS actively promote energy efficiency upgrades among landlo rds by offering them financial incentives, grants, and tailored support programmes specifically designed for rental properties. This approach effectively addresses the split incentives challenge that often arises when renovating buildings occupied by v ulnerable consumers, who are predominantly tenants. By incentivi sing landlords to invest in energy -saving measures, the HEEPS benefit both landlords and tenants.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: Landlords can take advantage of funding options and access resources provided through the HEEPS to enhance the energy efficiency of their rental properties, which may include insulation upgrades and the installation of energy-efficient heating systems. The Home Energy Efficiency Programme s for Scotland (HEEPS) have been successful in identifying and addressing barriers for renovation, making home improvements more accessible to a majority of consumers. Since its establishment in 2015, the Warmer Homes Scotland programme, a part of HEEPS, has had a significant impact by assisting almost 25 000 households in energy poverty.

passages.text: The primary objective of the ONPE is to collect accurate and widely shared information about energy poverty in France, with a specific focus on the housing sector and mobility. The primary goals of the ONPE are to provide a comprehensive and reliable perspective by producing accurate, consistent, and comparable data on both the phenomenon of energy poverty and the measures and financial assistance aimed to prevent and mitigate its impact. The ONPE also s erves as a platform for stakeholders to engage in national discussions, offering recommendations and proposals to address energy poverty.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: Furthermore, the ONPE plays a crucial role in sharing and raising awareness of its research findings through its regularly updated website, publications, dashboard, and diverse events. The ONPE's expertise has also served as a reference for the establishment of energy observatories in other countries such as Spain or Italy. What makes the energy poverty observatory a good practice? The ONPE brings together a range of professionals from various disciplines, including researchers, academics, policymakers, energy providers, social organisations, and other relevant actors. This is an important factor that contributes to the success of the network.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: The ONPE's network of experts enables the sharing of knowledge, experiences, and good practices related to energy poverty and provides decision -making support to government services, agencies, associations of energy suppliers and local authorities among others. The information is shared in a comprehensive way which facilitates its outreach to the general public. This structure enables the ONPE to bring expert advice and data-driven evidence to local and regional entities that are near vulnerable groups. This approach allows for a multidisciplinary approach that helps to understand and identify successful practices to tackle energy poverty in France229.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: From an organi sational perspective, the ONPE is supported by the French Agency f or Ecological Transition (ADEME)230, which is responsible for managing the secretariat and coordinating activities in collaboration with partners. The ONPE functions as a dynamic entity that addresses significant transition challenges by facilitating various working groups (WG). These working groups, including both permanent and ad hoc groups, play a crucial role in monitoring the ONPE's work. There are four permanent working groups. The Household-WG conducts surveys and research to understand the impact of e nergy poverty on households.

In addition to these groups, other WG can be created to respond to specific challenges such as the Europe -WG that searches to share the expertise of the ONPE with other European countries.

passages.text: 1 Introduction Article 26 addresses various aspects of decarbonising heating and cooling (H&C) supply. The main emphasis of this chapter is on district heating and cooling ( DHC) systems. Best practices are presented to support Member States in implementing the following aspects: • Voluntary use of labelling efficient DHC; • Linked increases of energy efficiency and usage of renewable energy; • Innovative approaches to developing DHC systems; • Integrated approaches to expanding DHC systems and energy efficiency; • Phasing out coal use in DHC systems; • Furthermore, three approaches to the calculation of the GHG emissions from (high-efficiency) cogeneration are presented.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: Lastly, the chapter goes into best practices for the conduct of costbenefit analyses (CBA) of various installations. 2 Voluntary uses of district heating labelling Articles 26(1) and 26(2) provide a definition of efficient DHC (EDHC) systems. The good practices presented in this section aim to present examples of Member States that have created labels to reflect the efficiency of DHC systems. The primary use of such labelling is to facilitate the administration of financial support. Other effects include stimulating competition between DHC operators and informing customers about the activities of their heating and cooling suppliers.

passages.text: 2 Incentives for efficient DHC systems In Germany, the definition of efficient DHC systems established by the previous version of the EED has been integrated in several German laws. The primary criterion is that the DHC system operates with a high share of renewable or waste heat. This share varies between different policies. For existing networks, the establishment of a plan to reach emission neutrality by 2045 is another key component. Through this integration into the legislation, the operator itself or other actors may benefit from being classified as ‘efficient’.

passages.text: 1 Introduction Article 29 strengthens the promotion of energy services by the Member States . This chapter presents good practices on support schemes for energy services, their quality labels, pub lic guarantees, integration to other energy efficiency measures . It looks at the specific application in buildings renovations and at the monitoring of measures related to energy services. 1 Common terms related to energy services Energy services markets in Europe feature a variety of contract types, many types of contractors (suppliers) and a few types of clients from the public and private sector. Latter traditionally includes industrial companies or tertiary buildings.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: So far, both of the most common contract types, Energy Performance Contracting and Energy Supply Contracting have been applied in nearly all sectors, including also residential and SME. The following box summarises the most common terms with respect to energy services and provides an overview of the various forms of energy services used in different contexts in Europe.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: Fraunhofer ISI | 126 Common terms related to energy services Energy Service means the physical benefit, utility or good derived from a combination of energy with energy-efficient technology or with action, which may include the operations, maintenance and control that are necessary to deliver the service on the basis of a contract and which under normal circumstances has proven to result in verifiable and measurable or estimable energy efficiency improvement or primary energy savings. Energy service provider is a natural or legal person who delivers energy services or other energy efficiency improvement measures in a final customer’s facility or premises.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: Performance-based energy services can be described as the general concept of an energy service, the quality of which is measured against a predefined performance guarantee. Energy efficiency service (EES): Agreed task or tasks designed to lead to an energy efficiency improvement and other agreed performance criteria. The EES shall include energy audits as well as identification, selection and implementation of actions and verification. A documented description of the proposed or agreed framework for the actions and the follow -up procedure shall be provided.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: The improvement of energy efficiency shall be measured and verified over a contractually defined period of time through contractually agreed methods [EN 15900:2010]. If the EES includes energy efficiency investments, it may or may not include financing of these investments. Partial services connected to energy efficiency services: Services that just include parts (“components”) of the EES value chain like design and implementation (excluding verification, for example), but that are designed to directly or indirectly lead to an energy efficiency improvement. If the partial EES includes EEI investments, it may or may not include financing of these investments.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: Energy performance contracting (E nPC) means a contractual arrangement between the beneficiary (or client) and the provider of an energy efficiency improvement measure, verified and monitored during the whole term of the contract, where investments (work, supply or service) in that measure are paid for in relation to a contractually agreed level of energy efficiency improvement or other agreed energy performance criterion, such as financial savings. A type of EnPC without major investments is sometimes called Operational Energy Contracting. Energy Supply Contracting (ESC) means a contractual arrangement for the efficient supply of energy.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: ESC is contracted and measured in Megawatt hours (MWh) delivered”. Integrated energy contracting (IEC) means a combination of energy efficiency measures with energy supply contracting typically with short term ‘operational verification’ rather than ongoing measurement and verification. Expanded energy service means a combination of EnPC with not only guaranteed cost savings from energy efficiency, but also from the provision of flexibility services. There is no clear definition, but according to Art. 29(4) such an extended energy service also includes demand response and energy storage services.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: Public private partnership (PPP) typically describes a long-term contractual arrangement for the provision of a public asset (such as energy efficiency investments) and related services (such as energy services) in exchange for performance-based payments linked to the asset’s availability and/or use and the delivery of the related services.

passages.text: 2 The (future) role of energy services in facilitating energy efficiency (and decarbonisation) investments On the way towards accelerating the energy transition, energy services can play a vital role by mobilising private capital for the investments at the consumer side. Energy services serve as an incentive for clients to engage in energy efficiency projects, allowin g them to shift organisational and, in some cases, financial burden to the service provider, the so-called Energy Service Company (ESCO). ESCOs have the necessary know-how to cover the whole service chain of energy efficiency projects, from choice of techn ology to installation and maintenance works.

passages.text: 2 Development of quality labels Various market surveys rev ealed the clear expectation of all market participants that quality assurance schemes for energy services would help to build trust in service providers and in this way positively influence the de mand for energy services298. Since energy services are complex, it is difficult for potential customers to distinguish projects with good quality from those with lower quality. In this context, quality assurance schemes can give neutral guidance to customers. However, the attempts to introduce quality assurance schemes in the Member States cannot yet be described as very successful until now.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: Several countries – such as the Czech Republic , Greece, Latvia, Slovenia, Slovakia, and Spain – have introduced schemes that evaluate the quality of energy service providers, generally based on technical and economic capacities as well as on the quality of reference projects299. According to available information, none of these schemes has achieved a high market penetration or a noticeable impact on the perceived quality of energy services. In Austria, for example, the Austrian Association of Energy Service Providers introduced a quality label for energy service projects in 2017. 300 However, this quality assurance scheme has received little attention from the market.

passages.title: Contractors' report on good practices related to the EED-Recast (Fraunhofer ISI, April 2024)
passages.text: The success of quality assurance schemes for energy services depends on a bundle of influencing factors. The perceived cost compared to the additional benefit attributed to quality assurance is clearly a limiting factor. Furthermore, the public awareness level about the scheme plays a crucial role, and given the fragmentation of energy services markets, it is a difficult and also cost-intensive task to increase awareness levels. Therefore, a strong public sector support is definitely required in the starting phase to ensure promotion and visibility so that quality assurance schemes are used by both energy service providers and customers. g. as part of a public programme).
